---
title: "Class diagrams: design before you type"
---

A base class, three subclasses, and a manager are five files, and not one of
them shows how the five fit together. A class diagram does. It fits on a
single page, and moving a method on it costs one line instead of three
files.

## Read a program from one picture {#sec-class-diagrams-read}

This is the bouncing balls from the inheritance chapter: three of its ball
kinds, and the game loop lifted out of `index.ts` into a class of its own.

![A bouncing-balls program on one page: five classes with their members, and
the two arrows that connect them.](balls-diagram.svg){width=610}

Answer these three from the picture. No editor, no files, no code.

1. Four of the five boxes are classes you could hand to `new`. One is not.
   Which one, and what in the picture says so?
2. `Game` keeps one array. What goes into it, and which of the three ball
   kinds may be pushed in?
3. Two members show up in `Ball` and again in every box below it. Name them,
   and say what that repetition means for the code.

You just read a design without opening a file. The notation that made it
readable comes next, and the answers with it.

## What one box says {#sec-class-diagrams-box}

![One class, three compartments. The name sits on top, the fields in the
middle, the methods at the bottom.](class-box.svg){width=470}

Every class is one box, split into three compartments stacked on top of each
other. Types are written the way TypeScript writes them, so a field line and
a method line are almost the code already. `(abstract)` behind the name means
the class is `abstract`, so `new Ball(...)` never compiles.

The character in front of a member says who may touch it:

* `+` is public. In this course that means no keyword at all, because public
  is the default.
* `-` is `private`, so only code inside that same class.
* `#` is `protected`, so the class and everything that extends it.

This notation is a small corner of UML, the Unified Modeling Language, which
software teams have drawn since the nineties. This book uses three pieces of
it: boxes, compartments, and two arrows.

A subclass box carries only what it adds or overrides, never the members it
inherited, and a box with nothing new in a compartment leaves that
compartment away. Types may go missing there too, once the parent box has
spelled them out.

## What the arrows say {#sec-class-diagrams-arrows}

Two arrows carry the bouncing-balls picture.

The **hollow triangle** is `extends`. The triangle sits at the base class, so
the arrow runs from `GummyBall` up to `Ball` and reads "GummyBall extends
Ball". The direction is worth learning: an arrow points from the class that
knows the other one to the class it depends on. `GummyBall` names `Ball` in
its very first line, and `Ball` never names `GummyBall`.

The **plain arrow with a label** covers everything else, which is one class
holding or using another. `Game` has a field of type `Ball[]`, so the label
reads "has many". A class that holds exactly one gets "has", a class that
only calls a method on another gets "uses". The label is prose, not syntax,
and its job is to tell the reader in three words what the field is for.

Back to the three questions. `Ball` is the class you cannot create, because
`(abstract)` stands behind its name. `Game` keeps a `Ball[]`, and all three
kinds fit into it, since every one of them extends `Ball`. And `bounciness`
and `onReachedBottom` show up four times each because they are abstract in
`Ball`, so every kind has to bring its own. That is exactly why one array and
one loop produce three different behaviors.

## The same picture as text {#sec-class-diagrams-mermaid}

Paper works, and paper is what you get in an exam. On a computer, mermaid
draws the picture from text you type:

```default
classDiagram
    class Ball {
        <<abstract>>
        #y: number
        #velocityY: number
        #radius: number
        +update(delta: number) boolean
        #onReachedBottom() boolean
    }
    Ball <|-- GummyBall
    Ball <|-- SteelBall
    Ball <|-- FragileBall
    Game --> Ball : has many
```

`<|--` draws the hollow triangle and `-->` the plain arrow. `<<abstract>>`
marks a class the same way the pictures above do. Paste the block into
[the mermaid live editor](https://mermaid.live) and the diagram appears next
to your text. Changing a design is then one line of typing, which beats an
eraser.

## An aquarium, on paper first {#sec-class-diagrams-aquarium}

Here is the program you build in the exercise below, described in five
sentences.

A `div` shows a photo of an aquarium. Fish are `<img>` elements placed inside
that photo at coordinates the program controls. Three kinds swim differently:
one straight left and right, one diagonally and bouncing off all four walls,
one left and right while riding a sine wave up and down. Every fish bounces
off the left and the right wall, turns its picture around when it changes
direction, and needs its own width to notice that it touched a wall. One
object owns the list of fish and runs the animation loop.

Before any of that turns into a file, it turns into this:

![The aquarium as five classes. `Fish` does everything the kinds share, and
`FishManager` never mentions a kind by name.](aquarium-diagram.svg){width=700}

Read the picture once and you know the program. `Fish` is abstract, so a
plain fish never exists. `step` is the only public method, so `FishManager`
can call nothing else. `update` is protected and abstract, so every kind
brings its own movement and nobody outside the family triggers it.
`keepInside` stands in `Fish` and again in `CrissCrossFish`, the one kind
that also bounces off the top and the bottom. `SinusFish` is the only box
with fields of its own.

Now turn one box into one file. Here is all of `FishManager`:

```ts
import type { Fish } from './fish';

export class FishManager {
  private fishes: Fish[] = [];
  private lastTime = 0;

  add(fish: Fish): void {
    this.fishes.push(fish);
  }

  start(): void {
    const tick = (timestamp: number) => {
      if (this.lastTime === 0) {
        this.lastTime = timestamp;
      }
      const delta = (timestamp - this.lastTime) / 1000;
      this.lastTime = timestamp;

      for (const fish of this.fishes) {
        fish.step(delta);
      }

      requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    };

    requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  }
}
```

The loop is the one from the animation chapter, with `delta` in seconds so
speeds are pixels per second. `Fish` appears here only as a type and never as
a value, so the import line is `import type`. And `tick` is an arrow function
for the reason the first chapter of this part gave: it borrows the `this`
around it, so `this.fishes` inside it still means the manager. Write
`function tick(...)` instead and `this` is gone by the time the browser calls
it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Draw it, then type it

The picture is free to change and the files are not. Notice on paper that
`keepInside` belongs in `Fish` and you move one line. Notice it after typing
and you rename a method, move it to another file, fix two imports, and run
the type check twice.
:::

::: {.research title="Placing a picture by hand, and asking it how big it is"}
The exercise below puts every fish at coordinates it computes itself, and a
fish cannot bounce off the right wall before it knows how wide it is.

1. `position: absolute` lets you place an element at a `left` and a `top` of
   your choice. Which `position` value does the surrounding `div` need so
   those coordinates count from the corner of the `div` instead of the corner
   of the page, and what does the browser use as the reference when no
   element around it has that value?
2. An `<img>` element has `naturalWidth` and `naturalHeight`. What do the two
   hold, why is `naturalWidth` still 0 in the line right after you set `src`,
   and which event tells you it is safe to read them?
3. `Math.sin(x)` returns a number between which two values, and what does the
   argument `x` stand for? Write the expression that turns it into a movement
   of 40 pixels up and down around the line `y = 200`.

For the exam, keep the two `position` values and how they work together in
your head. Placing something by hand comes back in every game you write.
:::

## Exercise: the aquarium {#sec-class-diagrams-exercise}

Build the program from the diagram above, and design a fish of your own
before you type a line.

{{< exercise aquarium >}}

1. **Draw it yourself.** Cover the aquarium picture above and draw the
   diagram from the five sentences that describe the program, on paper or in
   the mermaid live editor. Then add a fourth kind of fish of your own: one
   that swims in a circle, one that gets faster the further right it goes.
   For every member you write down, decide whether it belongs in `Fish` or in
   one kind. Then uncover the picture and compare. Expected result: the same
   members in the same boxes, or a reason why yours sit in better places.

2. **Look at what you copied.** `index.html` holds a heading, three buttons,
   and an empty `<div id="aquarium">`. `src/styles.css` gives that `div` its
   size and the background photo. Neither file needs a change yet.

3. **Two declarations from the research box.** In `src/styles.css`, add the
   one declaration to `#aquarium` that makes it the box a fish's coordinates
   count from. Then add a rule for `.fish` with the one declaration that lets
   an image sit at a `left` and a `top` of its own.

4. **The base class.** Create `src/fish.ts` with `export abstract class Fish`
   and the members from the `Fish` box:

   * The fields are the ones in the box, with their types. `width` and
     `height` start at 0 and `loaded` starts at `false`.
   * The constructor takes the aquarium element, the picture URL, `x`, `y`,
     `speedX`, and `speedY`. Store the four numbers in fields; the aquarium
     element becomes a `protected` field through a parameter property.
   * Still in the constructor, create an `<img>` with `createElement`, add
     the class `fish` to it, give it an `alt` text, and register a listener
     for the event from the research box. Inside that listener, set `width`
     and `height` to a third of the natural size, write both into
     `style.width` and `style.height` so the picture shrinks with them, and
     set `loaded` to `true`. Set `src` after the listener, and `append` the
     image to the aquarium.
   * `step(delta)` is public. While `loaded` is `false` it returns at once.
     Otherwise it calls `update(delta)`, then `keepInside()`, then `draw()`.
   * `update` is `protected abstract update(delta: number): void;` and has no
     body here.
   * `keepInside()` is protected. Read the aquarium's width with
     `this.aquarium.getBoundingClientRect().width`. When `x` is below 0, or
     when `x` plus the fish's width is past that edge, put the fish exactly
     on the edge and flip the sign of `speedX`.
   * `draw()` is private. Write `${this.x}px` into `style.left` and the same
     for `top`, and set `style.transform` to `scaleX(-1)` while `speedX` is
     negative and to `scaleX(1)` otherwise.

5. **The three kinds.** Create `src/horizontal-fish.ts`,
   `src/criss-cross-fish.ts`, and `src/sinus-fish.ts`, one class per file,
   each one `extends Fish` and each one with its own `update`. Speeds are
   pixels per second, so every movement is a speed times `delta`.
   `HorizontalFish` moves `x` only. `CrissCrossFish` moves `x` and `y`, and
   it also overrides `keepInside`: call `super.keepInside()` first, then do
   the same thing for the top and the bottom edge. `SinusFish` adds `baseY`
   and `time`, takes only one speed in its constructor and passes 0 as
   `speedY` to `super`, adds `delta` to `time` on every frame, and computes
   `y` from `baseY` and `Math.sin`, with the expression from the research
   box.

6. **The manager.** Create `src/fish-manager.ts` with the class printed
   above.

7. **Wire the page.** Replace `src/index.ts`. Import the stylesheet, import
   the six pictures from `/assets/fish1.png` to `/assets/fish6.png`, and
   import your four classes. Look up the `div` and the three buttons with
   `querySelector<...>` and one `if` that throws. Create one `FishManager`.
   Each button adds a fish of its kind: a random one of the six pictures, a
   start height between 20 and 320, and a speed between 40 and 100 pixels
   per second that is negative half of the time. Call `manager.start()` on
   the last line. Then run `npm start`.

   Expected result: each click drops a fish into the photo, it swims, it
   turns around at the wall, and its picture faces the way it swims. If the
   fish line up in a row in the top left corner and never move, step 3 is
   missing.

8. **Your own kind.** Add the fish you designed in step 1: a new file, a
   fourth button in `index.html`, and one more listener in `src/index.ts`.
   Expected result: your diagram from step 1 and your `src` folder now say
   the same thing.

9. Run `npm run verify` and fix what it reports.
